passage:
"Sarita didi, look! Mama gave me five hundred rupees for Diwali!" Vijay waved the note.
"Nice. What will you do with it?"
"Kaju katli. And jalebi. And the big box of chocolates at Sharma uncle's shop. All of it."
"All five hundred on sweets?"
"It's gift money. It's for fun."
Sarita raised an eyebrow. "Last week you wouldn't spend twenty from your pocket money on one samosa. You said you were saving."
"That's different! That's my money."
"Vijay, both are your money now."
He frowned at the note, then at his piggy bank on the shelf. "It doesn't feel the same, didi."
"Okay. Maybe half on sweets, and see how it feels?"
He thought about it. "Half. But the chocolates are in the first half."

qa.q: How much did Mama give Vijay for Diwali?
qa.a: Mama gave Vijay five hundred rupees for Diwali.

qa.q: Why does the gift money feel free to spend but the pocket money doesn't?
qa.a: To Vijay, gift money is "for fun" while pocket money is "my money" for saving; where the money came from changes how it feels, even though both are his.

qa.q: How could Sarita help Vijay think about the money without forcing him?
qa.a: She could keep asking gentle questions and offering a middle option, like the half-and-half idea, so he notices both notes are the same money and decides himself.

qa.q: How does Sarita see Vijay's plan?
qa.a: She finds it a bit funny and a bit silly that he treats the same rupees so differently, so she teases him kindly and points out both are his money.

grounding: It shows a boy ready to spend all his festival gift money on sweets while refusing to spend the same from his pocket money.

passage:
I'm Yogesh, and I'm nine. On Gudi Padwa, Aaji gave me, her only grandson, two hundred rupees in an envelope. I spent it the very same evening. Candy floss, a spinning top, gola, more gola. I didn't even think. It felt like money from the sky.
My sister Swati asked, "Why don't you spend your pocket money like that?" I have one hundred and fifty rupees in my tin from helping Baba wash the car on Sundays. I won't even buy a pencil with that. That money is heavy. I counted every coin.
Swati said, "But a rupee is a rupee." I know. But it doesn't feel like that. The envelope money felt light, like it wasn't really mine.
Now the gola is finished and I still have the tin.

qa.q: How much did Aaji give Yogesh on Gudi Padwa?
qa.a: Aaji gave Yogesh two hundred rupees in an envelope.

qa.q: Why did the envelope money feel "light" to Yogesh?
qa.a: It came as a gift, like money from the sky, so it didn't feel truly earned; the car-washing money felt heavy because every coin had been counted.

qa.q: What could Yogesh try the next time he gets festival money?
qa.a: Put it in the tin first and wait a day, then decide how much to spend, so he treats it the same as the money he earned.

qa.q: What might Swati be thinking when she says, "But a rupee is a rupee"?
qa.a: Swati probably finds it strange that the same money is spent so differently and is gently trying to show him that where money comes from doesn't change its worth.

grounding: It shows a boy who spends festival gift money freely on treats while guarding the same amount earned as pocket money.

Note to myself, after Eid
Irfan got his Eidi from everyone this year, about eight hundred rupees in all. By the evening he had spent almost all of it at the fair: sweets, a plastic sword, cotton candy, two rides. He was delighted and didn't hesitate once.
What struck me was the next day. At the stationery shop he wanted a new geometry box, and I said he could use his pocket money. He had more than enough in his jar. He shook his head. "No, Ammi, that's my saving money." He picked the box back up, looked at it for a long time, and put it down.
Same child, same rupees, but they clearly feel like two different kinds of money to him. I'll sit with him this week and see what he thinks about it.
Pooja

qa.q: How much Eidi did Irfan get this year?
qa.a: Irfan got about eight hundred rupees in all.

qa.q: Why did Irfan refuse to use his pocket money for the geometry box?
qa.a: Irfan feels protective of his jar because to him it is "saving money", while the Eidi felt like fun money, so the same rupees seemed to belong in different pots.

qa.q: How could Pooja help Irfan think about this without lecturing?
qa.a: She could ask him questions about why the two kinds of money feel different and let him work out that a rupee is a rupee, maybe by deciding together how to split next year's Eidi.

qa.q: What is it like for Pooja watching Irfan at the stationery shop?
qa.a: Pooja is curious and a little amused, noticing the same child treating the same rupees so differently, and wants to understand it with him.

grounding: It shows a boy who spends festival gift money freely but will not touch the same amount from his pocket money, seen by his mother.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today was Dashami, and my uncle Tapan gave me three hundred rupees for Puja! I went straight to the sweet shop with Chaitanya and bought rasgullas, sandesh, a big bag of jhalmuri and a toy gun that pops. All three hundred gone by six o'clock. Best day.
Then Chaitanya said, "Why don't you spend your piggy bank money on sweets too?" I said NO WAY. That's my saved money, ten rupees every Sunday from Baba since summer. Didi says I'm the richest boy in the house because of it. I would never waste it on sweets.
Chaitanya said, "But money is money." I said it's not the same. Puja money is for fun.
Now I'm in bed with a stomach ache and thinking. Is it the same? It doesn't feel the same.
Pradeep

qa.q: What did Pradeep buy with the Puja money?
qa.a: Rasgullas, sandesh, a big bag of jhalmuri and a toy gun that pops.

qa.q: Why does the piggy bank money feel different to Pradeep from the Puja money?
qa.a: Pradeep feels proud of the piggy bank money because he saved it slowly, ten rupees every Sunday, while the gift money came all at once and felt meant for fun.

qa.q: What could Pradeep try the next time he gets festival money?
qa.a: He could drop part of it into the piggy bank first and spend the rest, treating it like the money he works to save.

qa.q: Why might Chaitanya see the two kinds of money as the same?
qa.a: Chaitanya isn't attached to Pradeep's saving story, so three hundred rupees is simply three hundred rupees, whichever pot it sits in.

grounding: A boy spends all his festival gift money on sweets but would never spend his saved pocket money that way.

At the Pongal fair in their village near Thanjavur, Gopal had a hundred rupees from Thatha tied in his handkerchief. Before sunset it was gone: two rounds on the giant wheel, a paper windmill, and four packets of candy floss, one after another. On the way home his sister Minakshi said, "You still have forty rupees in your tin at home, from selling mangoes with Appa. Want to buy the flute you liked tomorrow?"
Gopal shook his head hard. "That's my mango money. I worked for it."
"It's the same rupees," Minakshi said.
"No it isn't," said Gopal, holding his sticky fingers away from his shirt.
Their mother, Sharmila, laughed quietly. "Same rupees, different feelings," she said.

qa.q: How much money did Thatha give Gopal?
qa.a: A hundred rupees, tied in his handkerchief.

qa.q: Why won't Gopal spend the mango money on the flute?
qa.a: He earned it selling mangoes with Appa, so it feels hard-won and precious, unlike Thatha's gift, which felt free to spend.

qa.q: What could Gopal try at the next fair?
qa.a: He could decide beforehand to keep some of the gift money in his tin, giving it the same care as money he earned.

qa.q: How might Minakshi see her brother's spending at the fair?
qa.a: Minakshi seems puzzled and a bit amused that Gopal spent a hundred rupees on candy floss but won't touch forty for a flute he really wanted.

grounding: A boy spends festival gift money freely at a fair but refuses to spend the smaller amount he earned himself.

passage:
Aunty's note, Christmas week.
Francis got five hundred rupees from his godparents this Christmas, and within an hour at the church fair he had spent nearly all of it: candyfloss, a plastic sword, three rounds of ring toss, plum cake for everyone. When his friend Tejas asked him to chip in fifty rupees for a new cricket ball, Francis refused. "That's from my pocket money. I'm saving that." I asked him what the difference was. He looked at me as if I was silly. "Gift money is for fun. Pocket money is real." We sat on the church steps and counted what was left: forty rupees of gift money. I asked which pile could have paid for the cricket ball. He frowned for a long time. Next week we'll talk about both piles together.

qa.q: How much did Francis get from his godparents?
qa.a: Five hundred rupees.

qa.q: Why did Francis feel free to spend the gift money but not his pocket money?
qa.a: Francis felt the gift money was playful and 'for fun', while pocket money felt real and worth protecting, even though both are the same rupees.

qa.q: What could help Francis think about the two piles more clearly?
qa.a: Talking it through with Aunty, as planned, seeing both piles as one amount and choosing together what matters most, like the cricket ball.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when Francis refused fifty rupees?
qa.a: Tejas might have felt puzzled or a bit hurt, having watched Francis spend freely on a sword and candyfloss.

grounding: Shows a child spending festival gift money freely while guarding pocket money, as if the source changed its value.

Diwali night
Total from all the uncles and aunties: 1,200 rupees! Diwali money isn't like normal money. It's MAGIC money. I spent the whole lot on sparklers, chocolates and the big rocket that went up once and fizzled. Didn't even feel bad.
Then Vinita asked if I'd lend her 100 for the craft fair. I said no, because I only had my pocket money left in the tin, and pocket money is SERIOUS money. I saved it for two whole months.
Vinita said, "But it's all just rupees, Nilesh." Hmm. If someone had asked me to spend 1,200 of my tin money on a rocket, I'd have said NO WAY. But I did exactly that. Just from the other pile.
Maybe I'll ask Papa to help me keep both in the same tin next year, so they feel the same.
Nilesh

qa.q: How much Diwali money did Nilesh get?
qa.a: Nilesh got 1,200 rupees from the uncles and aunties.

qa.q: Why didn't Nilesh feel bad spending the Diwali money?
qa.a: Nilesh felt happy and carefree, treating it as 'magic money' meant for fun, so spending it felt light, while tin money felt serious.

qa.q: Is Nilesh's idea of asking Papa for help a good one, and why?
qa.a: Yes; with Papa's help, keeping both in one tin could make them feel like the same money, so choices are made more evenly.

qa.q: How does Vinita see the two kinds of money?
qa.a: Vinita sees that it's all just rupees, whichever pile it comes from.

grounding: Shows a child spending all the festival money on fireworks while refusing to touch pocket money, because the source changes how money feels.

passage: At the Eid mela in Mandsaur, Harsha's pocket jingled with eidi from Nana, Mamu and three aunties: three hundred rupees. By sunset it was gone: jalebis, a spinning top, a balloon shaped like a fish, two rides on the giant wheel. Harsha didn't blink. But when his sister Ayesha wanted twenty rupees for bangles, he shook his head. "I only have my egg money left. That's from selling eggs every morning for a month." "It's twenty rupees, Harsha." "It's EGG money." Ayesha laughed. "You spent three hundred on a fish balloon and rides in one evening, and twenty is too much?" Harsha looked at the balloon, already sagging. Put that way, it did sound odd. He dug twenty out of his egg money and handed it over, slowly.

qa.a: Ayesha finds it funny and odd that three hundred rupees went on a fish balloon and rides but twenty for bangles felt like too much.

passage:
Daniel got money in birthday cards from his grandparents in Dublin: four crisp notes. "That's party money," he told his sister Leila, and by Sunday evening it was gone on sweets, stickers and a squishy toy shaped like a potato.

The next week, the ice-cream van came down their street. Leila had her pocket money ready.

"Want one?" she asked.

"Not with my pocket money," said Daniel. "That's saved money. It took me six weeks."

"Money's money," Leila said.

Daniel frowned and watched her lick her cone. It didn't feel the same at all. Birthday money felt light and fizzy. Pocket money felt heavy, like it had been earned.

qa.q: How many notes did Daniel get in birthday cards?
qa.a: Four crisp notes.

qa.q: Why did Daniel spend his birthday money quickly but refuse to use pocket money?
qa.a: The birthday money felt light and fun, so spending it felt carefree, but the pocket money felt earned and precious, so he felt reluctant to spend it.

qa.q: What could Daniel try next time he gets birthday money?
qa.a: He could decide with a parent before spending what he'd really like it for, as if it were his own saved money.

qa.q: How does Leila see Daniel's two kinds of money?
qa.a: Leila thinks money is just money and seems puzzled by why Daniel treats them so differently.

grounding: A child spends gift money freely on sweets but won't spend the same amount from his pocket money, because the source changes how it feels.

At the school fair in Class 5's corner, Imran had two envelopes. One held the Eid money his uncles had given him. The other held pocket money he'd saved from helping at his father's shop.

He spent the Eid money within half an hour: candyfloss, a lucky dip, a slushy that turned his tongue blue.

His classmate Lavanya pointed at a book stall. "That comic you wanted is there."

Imran touched the second envelope, then took his hand away. "That's my shop money. I don't want to use it."

"But you just spent more than that on candyfloss."

Imran looked at the empty Eid envelope and felt a strange twist in his stomach. "That was different," he said, not quite sure why.

qa.q: What did Imran spend the Eid money on?
qa.a: Candyfloss, a lucky dip and a slushy that turned his tongue blue.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he looked at the empty Eid envelope?
qa.a: He felt confused and a bit uneasy, sensing the two kinds of money weren't really different but not sure why they felt so.

qa.q: What would you advise Imran to do the next time he gets festival money?
qa.a: Before the fair, he could think about what he really wants, like the comic, and plan it together with a parent.

qa.q: How does Lavanya see Imran's choice?
qa.a: Lavanya thinks it doesn't make sense to spend a lot on candyfloss and then refuse to buy the comic.

grounding: A child spends festival gift money freely on sweets but guards his earned pocket money, because the source changes how it feels.

passage:
Diwali. Vaibhav got money from Dolma Aunty and three other relatives. He counted it on the bed and felt rich. "This is free money!"

Two days later. He'd spent almost all of it at the market on firecrackers and gulab jamun. He wasn't sorry. It had felt like a treat.

One week later. The school trip needed the same amount. Vaibhav had it in his piggy bank from months of pocket money, but he didn't want to break it. "That's my money," he told Mummy. "The Diwali money was different."

Mummy asked, "Wasn't it all your money?"

Vaibhav shook the piggy bank, heard the coins and felt a little foolish. He opened it for the trip.

qa.q: Who gave Vaibhav money at Diwali?
qa.a: Dolma Aunty and three other relatives.

qa.q: Why didn't Vaibhav want to break the piggy bank for the school trip?
qa.a: The piggy bank money felt earned and truly his, so he felt protective of it, while the Diwali money had felt free.

qa.q: What small step helped Vaibhav see his thinking?
qa.a: Mummy's question, "Wasn't it all your money?", helped him notice that the money was the same.

qa.q: How might Mummy see Vaibhav's two kinds of money?
qa.a: Mummy seems gently amused and wants him to see that all of it was his, however it came.

grounding: A child spends festival money freely but guards his pocket money, until he realises it is all the same.

passage:
Bhupen, you've spent all your Diwali money on crackers in one day? Let me tell you about your Mama when he was nine. I'm your Mahima Nani, and I remember it well.
That Diwali, his uncles gave him a hundred and fifty rupees in envelopes. He ran straight to the sweet shop and spent the whole lot on jalebis and barfi for his friends. "It's Diwali money," he said. "It's for fun."
The next week the ice-cream man came by. Your Mama had fifteen rupees of pocket money in his tin, saved from running errands. He wouldn't spend a single rupee. "That's my money," he said. "I earned it."
I asked him, "Isn't a rupee a rupee?" He stared at me as if I'd asked whether a cat was a dog.
He's an accountant now. He still laughs about it.

qa.q: How much Diwali money did the uncles give?
qa.a: The uncles gave a hundred and fifty rupees in envelopes.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen's Mama spend the Diwali money so freely?
qa.a: He felt happy and carefree, treating it as fun money, while his earned pocket money felt precious.

qa.q: Which question in the story could have changed how he saw the money?
qa.a: Nani's question, 'Isn't a rupee a rupee?', which points out that money is the same whatever its source.

qa.q: How might his friends have felt about the jalebis?
qa.a: His friends were probably delighted, enjoying treats bought with his Diwali money.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a boy who spent festival money freely but guarded the same amount from his pocket money.

passage:
On the second day of Losar, the market in Dharamshala was packed, and the last bus up the hill left in twenty minutes.
Tenzin had two kinds of money in two pockets. Left pocket: three hundred rupees from his uncles for Losar. Right pocket: eighty rupees he'd saved from selling old comics.
At the sweet stall the left pocket emptied fast: sesame sweets, a huge bag of candyfloss, fried dough for everyone. "It's Losar money," he told his sister Avni. "You're supposed to spend it."
Then Avni pointed at the bag shop. "Your school bag is torn. That one's seventy."
Tenzin's hand went to his right pocket and stopped. "That's my comic money. I'm saving it."
"It's all money, Tenzin."
The bus honked. They ran for it, Tenzin clutching candyfloss, his torn bag still on his back.

qa.q: How much Losar money did Tenzin have?
qa.a: Tenzin had three hundred rupees from his uncles for Losar.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin spend the Losar money but not the comic money?
qa.a: Tenzin felt happy and free spending the Losar money, while the comic money felt earned and precious, even though both were money.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do next time he has money from different places?
qa.a: Tenzin could think of it as one pot and decide with a parent what matters most, like the torn school bag.

qa.q: How does Avni see Tenzin's two pockets?
qa.a: Avni thinks it's all money and is a bit exasperated that the school bag stays torn.

grounding: Shows a child who spends festival gift money freely but will not touch the same kind of money he earned himself.

passage:
During the Christmas holidays in Mangaluru, Chaitanya got two hundred rupees in a card from Manjula Aunty. By evening it was gone: plum cake, a toy car and three packets of sugar-coated saunf. "Gift money is spending money," he declared.
Two days later, his mother asked him to put in fifty rupees for his little brother's birthday present. Chaitanya ran to his piggy bank, the one he fed every week from his pocket money, and hugged it. "Not this one! This is real money."
"The two hundred was real too," his mother said.
"That was different. It was a present."
She sat down with him and two scraps of paper. On one she wrote 200, on the other 50. "Which paper is more real?"
Chaitanya frowned at them for a long time.

qa.q: How much money did Manjula Aunty give?
qa.a: Manjula Aunty gave two hundred rupees in a card.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya hug the piggy bank?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt protective of the piggy bank money, which felt real and earned, while the gift money had felt free to spend.

qa.q: What did his mother do to help him think it through?
qa.a: She wrote 200 and 50 on two scraps of paper and asked which was more real, showing money is the same whatever its source.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya's mother feel about the vanished gift money?
qa.a: His mother seems patient and a little amused, using it as a gentle lesson rather than a scolding.

grounding: Shows a child who spends Christmas gift money freely but guards his pocket-money savings, as if the source changed the money.
